Meat-eating dinosaurs probably fed by dragging their teeth backward through flesh like a saw rather than biting straight down like a dagger, new experiments suggest.

Scientists at the University of Reading and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign found that the curved, serrated teeth of theropod dinosaurs needed about a third less force to cut when pulled diagonally backward than when pushed vertically downward.
The study, published Nov. 26 in Palaeontology , is the first to physically test how well these "steak knife" teeth cut.
Theropods are the group of dinosaurs that includes Allosaurus and Velociraptor, as well as modern birds. Many had flat, curved teeth with serrated front and back edges, similar to a steak knife.

To test how these teeth worked, the team built a new machine called the DinoSAW. It pushed a replica theropod tooth from an allosaur into ballistics gel, a material often used to mimic flesh, either straight down or at a diagonal backward angle. Sensors recorded the forces involved.

Dr. Manabu Sakamoto, a paleobiologist at the University of Reading who led the study, said, "We often picture meat-eating dinosaurs crunching straight down on their prey, but their teeth tell a different story. These teeth are curved backward and serrated on both edges, so we wanted to test whether pulling them through flesh worked better than biting down. It did, by a clear margin.

"This suggests these dinosaurs fed much like an eagle tearing at a carcass, sinking their teeth in and using their strong necks to pull back. It also means scientists modeling dinosaur skulls and teeth need to think about the direction of the bite, not just its strength.
"You might say this is the most cutting-edge dinosaur science ever conducted."

An aversion to artificial intelligence (AI) does not lessen the influence of the technology on people and their decision-making, according to new research from City St George's, University of London.

In a series of experimental studies on financial decision-making, the researchers found no difference in terms of how much participants were influenced by AI or humans, despite the majority of the participants expressing an antipathy to AI and a preference for advice from humans.
In a time when the sentiment about AI seems to be becoming more negative, the findings illustrate that perceiving AI advice as useful may trump people's expressed preferences.

The results—published in the journal Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin —also have practical implications, as, on the one hand, they illustrate the potential benefits of advice on issues such as finance, especially as financial advisers can be expensive.

However, they also highlight the potential risks of AI advice, as even people who express an aversion to AI may be influenced by AI recommendations. The authors add that disliking AI may therefore offer little protection against advice that serves interests other than their own, and that people and organizations using AI should take measures to avoid being influenced by misaligned or erroneous AI information.

To investigate the influence of and preference for humans or AI, the researchers—Constanza Musso and Dr. Andreas Kappes, senior lecturer in psychology at City St George's—recruited over 1,250 participants, who indicated their adviser preference and completed the same incentivized investment task while receiving advice from AI or human advisers.

In each experiment, participants made financial decisions for which they could earn or lose money. Before the experiment started, the researchers asked participants whether they would prefer to get advice from a human or an AI during their financial decision-making.

After seeing some information about investment alternatives and making an initial financial decision, they received advice from an AI or a human adviser, assigned randomly. Participants could then adjust their decision to make a final investment. Each participant made several investment decisions, and they could earn or lose money as a result of their choices.

Sweden has been ranked the world's leading supporter of international media freedom, according to a new index. The index also highlights a decline in funding from 30 leading donor countries, despite growing threats to independent journalism worldwide.
The Index on International Media Freedom Support (IMFS) evaluates countries on how actively they support media freedom beyond their borders through diplomatic, funding and safety efforts.
It is published annually by an independent team of academics at the University of East Anglia (UEA) and City St George's, University of London.
Sweden topped the 2026 index—moving up one place from 2025—largely due to its significant financial support for international media development.
In 2024, Sweden spent 1. 01% of its total aid budget on supporting independent journalism around the world.
However, Sweden is an outlier. Across all 30 countries in the index, just 0. 15% of official development assistance (ODA) was allocated to media support in 2024, down from 0. 16% in 2023.
Three countries gave no money at all to international media development—despite having pledged to promote media freedom internationally: Latvia (18th), Greece (24th) and Slovenia (29th).

Report author Martin Scott, a professor from UEA's School of Global Development, said, "At a time of growing geopolitical instability and mounting pressure on independent media, international support should be increasing, not declining."

A team of archaeologists and scientists has uncovered tantalizing new evidence that Late Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago—nearly a millennium earlier than currently confirmed.

A study published Nov. 26 in the Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy combines new excavations at Ballynamintra Cave, near Dungarvan in County Waterford, with a modern scientific reassessment of animal bones originally dug from the cave in 1878–1882 and curated at the National Museum of Ireland.

Until now, the earliest firm evidence for people in Ireland prior to the Mesolithic has been a single butchered brown bear bone from Alice and Gwendoline Cave in County Clare, dating to roughly 12,800–12,600 years ago. By contrast, hunter-gatherers had already reached Britain after the Last Glacial Maximum by around 15,000 years ago as the last ice sheets retreated.

Re-examining the 19th-century Ballynamintra Cave collection, the researchers identified two extinct giant deer (Megaloceros giganteus) leg bones bearing marks consistent with human butchery while the bones were still fresh.

One upper foreleg bone (top image) shows a uniform chopping plane consistent with a heavy-bladed stone tool used to hack the elbow joint apart, alongside wolf gnaw marks suggesting carnivores later scavenged the carcass. A lower hindleg bone (see image below) shows a possible stone-tool percussion impact and microfractures caused by splitting the fresh bone open to extract nutrient-rich marrow. High-precision radiocarbon dating at the University of Oxford dated this bone to 13,573–13,321 years ago.

Because surface weathering over millennia erased microscopic tool striations, the researchers caution that the marks cannot yet be proven as definitively human-made without additional artifacts. However, the timing aligns directly with contemporary hunter-gatherer activity across Britain and northwest Europe during a warm Ice Age interval known as the Middle Allerød.

Crucially, the team's excavations in the cave's entrance chamber overturned a century-old assumption that Victorian antiquarians had completely emptied Ireland's "bone caves." Working in an intact section of cave sediment, the team recovered previously undisturbed Ice Age layers containing three giant deer specimens and a red fox jawbone radiocarbon dated to between 13,604 and 13,095 years ago, alongside preserved ancient pollen indicating an open grassland landscape fringed by ferns, juniper and birch.

"Confirming human activity at Ballynamintra Cave 13,500 years ago would significantly push back the arrival of people in Ireland and reshape how we understand early human dispersal across northwest Europe at the end of the last Ice Age," said Dr. Richard Jennings, School of Biological and Environmental Sciences, Liverpool John Moores University, who led the study.

Experimental archaeology sheds light on the substances fermented in Neolithic Scandinavian pottery and deposited in tombs, suggesting fermented dairy products held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.

Fermentation was likely important to early farming communities in northern Europe (c. 3300–2800 B. C. ), helping to preserve food, create desirable flavors and, in the case of milk, reduce lactose and thereby make dairy products easier to digest.
In southern Scandinavia, corrosion on ceramic vessels indicates they were used for fermentation. However, identifying fermented foods in archaeological pottery is difficult.

"Pottery has been central to our understanding of Neolithic communities in southern Scandinavia," says the study's lead author, Lone Claudi-Hansen, from the University of Copenhagen and Museum Vestsjælland. "Yet we know little about what these pots contained and how they were used."
To tackle this, researchers gathered 330 Middle Neolithic pottery vessels from passage tombs, settlements and wetlands in western Zealand, Denmark, and examined them for traces of corrosion.
They found that 29 of the 31 vessels with corrosion traces came from passage tombs, suggesting that fermented substances played a role in funerary rituals.

"Some of the finest and most elaborately decorated pottery of the Neolithic was deposited in passage tomb chambers and outside passage tomb entrances, but was it the vessels themselves or their contents that mattered?" asks Claudi-Hansen.

To answer this, they created reconstructions of Neolithic pottery and filled them with various foodstuffs available to Neolithic communities, such as milk, beer, vinegar and mead. After leaving the contents in the vessels for an extended period, they compared the corrosion to that on the Neolithic vessels. Their results are published in the journal Antiquity .

articles.title: Scientists Discover 130-Year-Old Fish Still Swimming in an American River
articles.dek: Some fish swimming in Montana’s Upper Missouri River today may have hatched before the 20th century began.
paragraphs: Some fish swimming in Montana’s Upper Missouri River today may have hatched before the 20th century began. Researchers have confirmed that blue suckers can live up to 130 years, more than three times their previously estimated lifespan of roughly 40 years. The discovery places the species among the longest-lived vertebrates in North America.

The findings, published in Communications Biology , come from a study co-led by Alec Lackmann of the University of Minnesota Duluth, Luke Holmquist of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews of the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa. By examining microscopic structures inside the fishes’ heads and using a chemical signature left by nuclear weapons testing, the scientists uncovered evidence of extraordinary longevity and a population increasingly dominated by old individuals.

The blue sucker ( Cycleptus elongatus ) is native to 23 U. S. states but is classified as imperiled in 22 of them. For decades, researchers monitoring the Upper Missouri River have observed increasingly large fish and remarkably few juveniles. The pattern suggests that young blue suckers have struggled to survive and join the adult population.

“For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range,” the researchers wrote. “Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap.”

To investigate, the team collected and examined nearly 50 blue suckers between 2023 and 2026. More than 60 percent were older than 90 years, and some had survived for approximately 130 years. Their age distribution suggests that successful recruitment of new generations has become less frequent since major dams were installed in the mid-1900s. Habitat fragmentation associated with those dams is a possible contributor, although the study does not establish it as the cause.

The researchers determined the fishes’ ages by examining otoliths, tiny structures commonly called earstones that occur in approximately 97 percent of fish species. These structures grow throughout a fish’s life, accumulating annual layers that scientists can count under a microscope, much like the growth rings of a tree.

Blue suckers presented a technical challenge because their otoliths are exceptionally small. “Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them,” Lackmann said.

As the researchers examined the growth layers, they encountered ages that far exceeded established expectations. In fish previously thought to live around four decades, “we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old,” Lackmann said. “When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity.”

To independently verify the ages, the team turned to bomb radiocarbon dating, a technique that uses the atmospheric changes caused by nuclear weapons testing during the Cold War. Those tests produced a distinctive increase in radioactive carbon-14 that became incorporated into living organisms, including the tissues of fish.
“Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere,” said Lackmann.

“This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you’re able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc. ) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate. Bomb radiocarbon dating is one of the best ways to age-validate long-lived organisms. So that’s where we have multiple lines of evidence here, otoliths providing the age estimates, and bomb radiocarbon confirming and validating the otolith ages and extreme longevity of the blue sucker.”

By comparing the carbon-14 signatures in the otoliths with the known timing of the atmospheric radiocarbon increase, the researchers validated the ages estimated from the growth layers. This independent evidence confirmed that blue suckers can survive for more than a century.

The blue sucker is now the fourth member of the sucker fish family (Catostomidae) found to reach 100 years or older, joining the bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo, and black buffalo. All four species have had their exceptional longevity documented since 2019, partly through advances in fish aging techniques.

Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

What if you could build almost anything you imagined simply by designing a set of tiny building blocks, putting them in a container and shaking them until they assembled themselves into the desired shape?
It sounds a bit like playing Minecraft. But instead of constructing virtual worlds with digital cubes, researchers are bringing that concept to life at a scale almost unimaginably small—using DNA.

In research published in Science Robotics , associate professor Sulc and his team in ASU's School of Molecular Sciences and the Biodesign Center for Molecular Design and Biomimetics introduce a new platform that uses specially designed, cube-shaped DNA structures as building blocks.

These microscopic cubes can spontaneously assemble into complex, three-dimensional (3D) structures, offering a new approach to one of nanotechnology's longstanding challenges: how to reliably build intricate objects at the nanoscale without having to position each component individually.
"It's like playing Minecraft at a very, very small scale," Sulc says.

The analogy captures the central idea behind the research. Rather than painstakingly placing each component in its proper position, researchers design the building blocks and the interactions between them so that, when mixed together in solution, they find one another and assemble into a predetermined structure.

The result is a programmable construction system that could eventually make it possible to create complex nanoscale objects with applications ranging from reconfigurable nanorobots to three-dimensional electronic circuits.

articles.title: Intermittent Fasting May Not Work the Way Scientists Thought for Liver Health
articles.dek: A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.
paragraphs: A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.

For people using intermittent fasting to reduce fat in the liver, finding a meal schedule that helps them lose weight may be more important than eating at specific times of the day. A new clinical trial found that people who lost at least 5% of their body weight experienced the greatest reductions in liver fat, with no clear advantage to eating earlier or later in the day.

Led by the University of Granada (UGR) and the Public University of Navarra, the multicenter study was published in JHEP Reports and involved 197 adults aged 30 to 60 with overweight or obesity. The research forms part of the doctoral dissertation of Antonio Clavero Jimeno, a predoctoral researcher at the University Joint Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at UGR.

The researchers conducted a secondary analysis of a clinical trial previously published in Nature Medicine . That trial found that participants who practiced intermittent fasting lost an average of 3 to 4 kilograms (6. 6 to 8. 8 pounds) more than those who received only nutritional recommendations, regardless of their eating schedule. Eating earlier in the day, which in Spain often amounts to skipping dinner, also produced specific improvements in certain measures of blood sugar regulation.

To investigate whether these eating schedules offered additional benefits for liver health, the researchers compared three forms of time-restricted eating (TRE), a type of intermittent fasting that confines food consumption to specific hours of the day.

Participants were randomly assigned to four groups: standard care, early eating (approximately 9 a. m. to 5 p. m. ), late eating (2 p. m. to 10 p. m. ), and a self-selected eating window (12:20 p. m. to 8 p. m. on average). Over 12 weeks, all four groups received the same nutritional education program based on the Mediterranean diet and healthy lifestyle habits.

The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure liver fat and examined liver stiffness, liver enzymes, circulating proteins involved in liver metabolism, and other indicators of liver health.

Although liver fat decreased in all three intermittent fasting groups, none experienced statistically significant improvements beyond those achieved through standard care. The timing of meals also made no significant difference to other measures of liver health or the composition and diversity of microorganisms living in the gut.

Approximately 40 to 45% of participants practicing intermittent fasting lost at least 5% of their body weight. Reaching this threshold was associated with significantly greater reductions in liver fat, and most participants who achieved it belonged to the fasting groups. Greater reductions were also observed among people who already had hepatic steatosis, an excessive accumulation of fat in the liver, at the beginning of the study.

“The results do not suggest that intermittent fasting is ineffective, but rather that choosing an early, late, or self-selected fasting window does not appear to provide any additional benefit for liver health,” explain Manuel Dote Montero and Antonio Clavero Jimeno, the study’s first authors.
For the researchers, “the most important factor seems to be choosing a strategy that facilitates clinically significant weight loss and can be sustained over time.”

articles.title: Scientists Uncover a Potential Root Cause of the Global Allergy Epidemic
articles.dek: Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.
paragraphs: Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.

Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system. An extensive analysis led by Griffith University researchers challenges decades of conventional thinking about allergic diseases and proposes a potential biological origin for conditions ranging from eczema to food allergies.

The researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function. Their findings suggest that epithelial cells, which form protective barriers along the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus, may struggle to meet environmental and metabolic demands, triggering an excessive immune response.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” said study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist from Griffith’s School of Medicine and Dentistry.

The team examined what it describes as the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data known to the researchers, drawing on 116 case-control cohorts and data from 3,776 patients. Multi-omic analysis combines different types of molecular information to identify biological patterns that might otherwise go undetected.
Scientists may have discovered the hidden cause of allergies. Credit: Professor Peter Smith, Griffith University

“Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces,” Professor Smith said.
“The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow.
“It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions.”

The strongest evidence emerged in eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic inflammatory disease affecting the esophagus. Across all 13 independent patient cohorts, researchers found reduced activity in the cellular process responsible for removing damaged mitochondria.

In patients with eczema, abnormalities affecting the skin’s protective barrier and antioxidant defenses appeared even in areas without inflammation. This finding is consistent with the possibility that cellular dysfunction precedes visible symptoms.
However, the mitochondrial signature was not universal. Researchers found only partial evidence of it in hay fever, while the pattern was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps.

The researchers propose that several environmental factors associated with allergies could converge on the same biological vulnerability: the ability of epithelial cells to generate sufficient energy and withstand stress.
Potential contributors include highly processed diets, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure early in life.

articles.title: Losing Weight but Getting Less Healthy? Study Reveals a Dark Side of Keto
articles.dek: Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.
paragraphs: Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.

Ketogenic diets have become a popular approach to weight loss, despite conflicting research on their metabolic benefits. A new study in mice suggests that two often overlooked factors may help explain these inconsistencies: the amount of protein in the diet and the genetic makeup of the animals eating it. The findings also raise questions about whether losing weight on a keto diet necessarily means becoming healthier.

The research, published in Cell Metabolism , began when first author Zhaoyue Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow in the Friedman lab, noticed considerable variation in the protein content of ketogenic diets. Although these diets are generally high in fat and extremely low in carbohydrates, their protein content could be contributing to differences in metabolic outcomes.

Zhang and her colleagues systematically tested diets containing different proportions of fat and protein. After four weeks on a ketogenic diet containing just 5% protein, mice belonging to C57Bl/6J, the most commonly used laboratory mouse strain, reduced their food intake by approximately 40% and lost weight. Mice fed an otherwise similar diet containing 10% protein ate more and gained weight. Both groups produced ketones, molecules generated when the body relies heavily on fat for fuel, suggesting that ketosis alone could not account for the difference.

A closer look at the mice that lost weight revealed a more complicated picture. Although their glucose tolerance, or ability to manage changes in blood sugar, improved, they also developed fatty liver. Much of their weight loss was associated with reductions in lean mass, including muscle.

To understand what was suppressing the animals’ appetite, the researchers investigated GDF15, a hormone released in response to cellular stress that can act on the brain to reduce food intake. When they conducted an experiment using genetically modified mice lacking GDF15, even the control mice unexpectedly failed to lose weight on the low-protein diet.
“At first, I was a bit panicked,” Zhang says. “We had repeated the same experiment many times, and all of a sudden it didn’t work.”

Retracing her steps, Zhang discovered that the genetically modified mice belonged to a different substrain, C57Bl/6N, which shares approximately 99. 9% of its genome with the mice used in the earlier experiments.
“This realization was key, and it became the starting point for the rest of the study,” Zhang says.

The researchers eventually identified two genes that helped explain the difference: NNT, which protects cells against oxidative stress, and NLRP12, which helps regulate inflammation. The mice susceptible to weight loss, known as B6J, carried mutations in both genes. Feeding them the low-protein ketogenic diet triggered stress and inflammatory responses in the liver, accompanied by rising levels of GDF15 and an inflammation-associated protein called LCN2. Both proteins can influence appetite through their effects on the brain.

Restoring NNT function in B6J mice caused them to eat more and lose less weight. Conversely, disabling both genes in the genetically similar B6NJ mice, which normally carry functioning versions of both genes, caused them to eat less and lose weight. Treatment with N-acetylcysteine, an antioxidant with anti-inflammatory properties, also lowered circulating levels of GDF15 and LCN2, increased food intake, and reduced weight loss.

Zhang cautions that the findings cannot be directly applied to humans, particularly because the 5% protein diet contained substantially less protein than most ketogenic diets used in clinical trials. Future trials could benefit from paying closer attention to both dietary protein content and genetic differences among participants, while looking beyond weight loss and blood sugar control when assessing metabolic health.
The researchers now want to investigate whether other genetic factors influence responses to ketogenic diets and whether the changes they observed can be reversed once the diet is discontinued.

articles.title: NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement
articles.dek: How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions…
paragraphs: How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace.

NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

“We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”

Under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

“Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”
Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

“GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” said Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”
NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

articles.title: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus
articles.dek: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from…
paragraphs: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.
Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

But looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.
Many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

Before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.
The researchers found that while the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.
Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.
Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

articles.title: Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard
articles.dek: Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood.
paragraphs: Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

“I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

“I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.
When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

“Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she said, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”
As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test plans, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U. S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

“While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” said Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”
The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

articles.title: Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried
articles.dek: Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global…
paragraphs: Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A new study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

The characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

The study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

“This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang said.
Aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

Water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

To put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

“This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang said. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”

articles.title: America’s Data Centers Have a Hidden Death Toll, MIT Researchers Warn
articles.dek: An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than…
paragraphs: An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.

As artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension. The electricity needed to keep these facilities running around the clock can increase air pollution in communities far from where the data centers themselves are built, potentially putting the health of people who live nowhere near them at risk.

Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone. Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas had the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita, even though much of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Rates in Virginia and Texas were only about half those in most Midwestern states.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, senior author of the study, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), and director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers’ electricity needs accounted for about 4 percent of total U. S. energy demand in 2023 and approximately 4. 4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. Those proportions have likely grown as more facilities have been built.

Determining who bears the health consequences of that growing demand is complicated by the interconnected nature of the nation’s power grid. A data center in Virginia, for example, may increase electricity production at power plants in the Ohio Valley, where a greater proportion of older coal and natural gas plants produce higher levels of emissions.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

The pollution can then travel into neighboring states, where local atmospheric conditions can make matters worse. In agricultural regions such as Iowa and Nebraska, ammonia released from fertilizer promotes the formation of fine particulate matter (PM 2. 5 ), microscopic airborne particles that can cause heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

The estimated health consequences also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas. Overall, the researchers found that rural populations face a significantly higher estimated mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations.

To understand how these risks are distributed, the team developed a model that tracks electricity production and transmission between regions on an hourly basis. While many previous studies relied on average power grid emissions, the researchers assumed that data centers operated around the clock and identified which individual generators would respond to their additional electricity needs.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” says Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student and co-author of the study.

“It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U. S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”

The researchers calculated emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide from individual generators. Both pollutants contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter, while nitrogen oxides also help produce ground-level ozone, commonly associated with smog.

Using a separate atmospheric model, the team simulated how these pollutants formed and traveled across regions. They then drew on epidemiological research linking air pollution to premature death to estimate the resulting health impacts.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Views Ocean of Stars in Groundwork for Roman
articles.dek: An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way.
paragraphs: An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way. The images focus on an area of sky toward the galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of a galaxy’s disk. These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

Astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail. Although we can see the glow from these crowded spheres of stars in other galaxies, they are too jam-packed and far away to resolve individual stars. By studying the Milky Way’s galactic bulge, researchers hope to find new planets and better understand how galaxies form, evolve, and interact over billions of years.

Hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light. Because researchers wish to compare Hubble’s observations to future Roman observations, Hubble looked at the region in wavelengths that overlap with Roman’s areas of sensitivity, the red end of the visible spectrum and near-infrared wavelengths.

Hubble’s high resolution allows its instruments to collect data on the brightness, ages, composition, and motion of stars over time. With this knowledge, astronomers can search for potential exoplanets, determine the location of black holes or dark matter, and better understand our galaxy’s environment and evolution.

A key component of Roman’s future observations is the search for exoplanets by capturing microlensing events , a type of gravitational lensing that occurs when light from a more distant object is magnified and distorted by the mass of a closer object along the line of sight. The way light from the distant star is distorted and magnified can reveal clues to the nature of the foreground star and any planets it may have. Hubble’s observations will help characterize stars in the region before they undergo a lensing event. Months or years in the future, when Roman captures a microlensing event, researchers can compare Hubble data to Roman data of the event, making it easer to interpret.
These microlensing events are on a much smaller scale, that of stars and planets, than larger gravitational lenses that occur around galaxies and galaxy clusters .

Over Hubble’s lifetime, it has observed our galaxy’s central bulge many times. These legacy surveys include the WFC3 Galactic Bulge Treasury Program that used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 to study the brightness, precise positions, and motions of stars in this congested part of our galaxy. It also includes the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search (SWEEPS) that used Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys to look at 180,000 stars in the bulge of our galaxy. These new observations come from an observing program (# 17776 : S. Terry) designed to aid Roman in its search for exoplanets, black holes, neutron stars, and more.
The data also adds to Hubble’s continuing legacy of high-precision observations of stars in the galactic bulge.
Claire Andreoli NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center , Greenbelt, MD claire. andreoli@nasa. gov
Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.
Hubble’s most notable scientific discoveries reflect the broad range of research and the breakthroughs it has achieved.
NASA’s Hubble and Roman space telescopes will work together to broaden our perspective of the universe.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will settle essential questions in the areas of dark energy, exoplanets, and astrophysics.

articles.title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
articles.dek: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once…
paragraphs: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.
My anthropology colleague Sissel Schroeder and I studied both sites to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.

During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as mismanaged drainage infrastructure . Yet in interviews with a community group, residents reported that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came.

From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by 10 inches (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more frequent flooding , including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which back up raw sewage into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.

Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes . Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.

Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound.

Monks Mound is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears – timber monuments likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing elaborate burials .

Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that continued for 200 years . Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a range of societal and environmental theories .

In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that Cahokia experienced several natural disasters during a warming period known as the Medieval Climatic Anomaly . In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to those climatic changes .

Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow .” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.

As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, archaeological evidence suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: Larger houses and status symbols became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor.
To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.

People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “ I’m not going to abandon my house . It’s all I got.”

Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.

At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were most exposed to crop loss from flooding , but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.

People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to communal feasts and shared food storage . I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society.
If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; some benefited, some lost , and some left .

Today, some consequences of climate change can be major and immediate, such as sudden massive floods . But in communities like Centreville, the effects of repeated flooding accumulate over years, producing gradual societal changes that are harder to recognize than the aftermath of a sudden catastrophe.

Climate models are useful for estimating future conditions, but they reveal nothing about how people might experience or respond to those conditions. Events and people’s reactions may unfold quickly, even suddenly, or they may play out quietly over long periods of time.
Regardless, the result may be the stillness of an archaeological site.
